content: Bipedalism refers to the ability to stand or move using two appendages, typically legs. Animals or machines that primarily use this form of locomotion are called bipeds, derived from the Latin words bi (two) and ped (foot). Types of Bipedal Movement 1. Standing: This involves remaining stationary on both legs. For most bipeds, maintaining balance while standing is an active process that requires constant adjustments. 2. Walking: This is characterized by placing one foot in front of the other, ensuring that at least one foot is always in contact with the ground. 3. Running: In this form of movement, one foot is placed in front of the other, but there are moments when both feet are off the ground simultaneously. 4. Hopping: This involves moving by jumping, with both feet leaving and landing on the ground together. Bipedal Animals Bipedal locomotion has evolved multiple times across different species, particularly among vertebrates. Birds are the most prominent example, having inherited bipedalism from their theropod dinosaur ancestors. All dinosaurs are believed to have descended from a fully bipedal ancestor, possibly resembling the early dinosaur Eoraptor. Among modern birds, large flightless species like ostriches exemplify bipedal efficiency, capable of reaching speeds up to 65 km/h. Similarly, many theropod dinosaurs, such as maniraptors, likely achieved comparable speeds. Bipedalism also re-emerged in other dinosaur lineages, such as the iguanodons. Some extinct crocodilian relatives, like Effigia okeeffeae from the Triassic period, also exhibited bipedal locomotion. Among modern birds, larger species tend to walk using alternating legs, while smaller birds often hop. Penguins are unique in their upright posture, which contrasts with the horizontal body orientation of most other birds. In mammals, bipedalism is less common, as most are quadrupedal. However, kangaroos and their relatives are notable exceptions, primarily using hopping as their mode of movement. Other examples include hopping rodents like kangaroo rats and springhares. Certain primates, such as sifakas and sportive lemurs, also hop when on the ground. Gibbons and giant pangolins are among the few mammals, aside from humans, that use an alternating bipedal gait rather than hopping. Some mammals, like bonobos and proboscis monkeys, adopt a bipedal stance when wading through water. Occasionally, these primates, along with others, may walk or stand bipedally on land. Other animals exhibit limited forms of bipedalism. For instance, rats may squat on their hind legs to manipulate food, while raccoons often stand erect or squat in water to handle objects. Beavers may move bipedally when carrying branches. Bears can rise and move bipedally during confrontations to better utilize their forelimbs as weapons. Ground squirrels and meerkats stand on their hind legs to survey their surroundings, but they do not walk bipedally. Gerenuk antelopes stand on their hind legs to browse leaves from trees, a behavior also observed in the extinct giant ground sloth and possibly in the chalicotheres, an extinct group of rhinoceros-like mammals. An unusual example of bipedalism is seen in the spotted skunk, which, when threatened, stands on its forelimbs to aim its anal glands at an attacker. This defensive posture allows the skunk to spray a foul-smelling oil while maintaining visual contact with the threat. Bipedalism is virtually absent among amphibians and rare among non-archosaur reptiles. However, certain lizards, such as the basilisk lizard, can run bipedally, even across water surfaces. Some insects, like cockroaches, exhibit bipedal running, but bipedalism is otherwise unknown in arthropods. While most bipeds are terrestrial, at least two species of octopus have been observed walking bipedally on the seafloor. This form of locomotion may help them remain camouflaged while moving, as they can use their remaining arms for disguise, mimicking objects like coconuts or seaweed. This movement is thought to require minimal brain control. Exceptional Cases Animals that do not naturally use bipedal locomotion can sometimes be trained to walk on their hind legs. Animals with limb injuries or congenital deformities may adapt to bipedal movement, either on two hind legs or on one front and one back leg. For example, some dogs have been observed walking bipedally due to such adaptations. Rare cases of bipedalism have also been documented in primates. A captive macaque named Natasha switched to exclusively bipedal walking after recovering from a severe illness. Similarly, a captive chimpanzee named Oliver was known to walk upright consistently. Some animals can also be trained to walk on their forelimbs, as seen in handstand walking by humans. Advantages of Bipedalism 1. Improved Perception: Standing upright enhances the ability to see distant dangers or resources, which may have been a critical evolutionary advantage for some species. 2. Free Forelimbs: In vertebrates, bipedalism frees the front limbs for other functions, such as manipulation (in primates), flight (in birds), digging (in pangolins), or combat (in bears). 3. Wading: Some animals, like raccoons and certain primates, adopt a bipedal stance in water, allowing them to stand or walk in deeper water while keeping their heads above the surface. 4. Faster Movement: In animals with rigid backbones, such as lizards or cockroaches, bipedalism can increase running speed. However, the maximum speed of bipedal movement is generally slower than that of quadrupedal movement in animals with flexible backbones. For example, the fastest bipeds, such as ostriches (65 km/h) and red kangaroos (70 km/h), are slower than the fastest quadruped, the cheetah (103 km/h). 5. Greater Reach: Gerenuk antelopes use a bipedal stance to access leaves on trees that would otherwise be out of reach. 6. Camouflage: Bipedal movement in octopuses may allow them to remain camouflaged while moving, as they can use their other arms for disguise. 7. Defensive Posture: The spotted skunk’s ability to walk on its forelimbs while aiming its anal glands at an attacker is a unique defensive adaptation. Evolution of Bipedalism Bipedalism has evolved independently in various lineages due to its adaptive advantages. Early Reptiles and Lizards The earliest known biped is Eudibamus cursoris, a bolosaurid reptile from 290 million years ago. Its long hind legs, short forelimbs, and specialized joints suggest bipedal locomotion, likely for increased speed. This species became extinct before the appearance of dinosaurs. Some modern lizards, such as basilisks, have independently developed the ability to run bipedally for speed. Dinosaurs and Birds Bipedalism evolved independently in dinosaurs. The earliest dinosaurs, such as Eoraptor, were small, bipedal predators. Fossil evidence from related species like Marasuchus and Lagerpeton supports the idea that the first dinosaurs were bipedal. Birds inherited bipedalism from their theropod ancestors. Mammals (Excluding Humans) Some mammals adopt bipedal stances for specific purposes, such as feeding or fighting. Groups like macropods (kangaroos and relatives) evolved bipedal hopping as their primary mode of locomotion. Humans, whose bipedalism has been extensively studied, are discussed separately. Humans Human bipedalism likely evolved before the expansion of brain size. Multiple hypotheses attempt to explain its origins, including: Postural Feeding Hypothesis: Suggests that early hominins became bipedal to reach food in trees or on the ground. Provisioning Model: Proposes that bipedalism evolved to allow males to carry food back to their families in a monogamous society. Thermoregulatory Model: Argues that bipedalism reduces heat gain and improves heat dissipation by exposing less body surface to direct sunlight. Carrying Models: Suggests that bipedalism evolved to free the hands for carrying tools, weapons, or infants. Wading Hypothesis: Proposes that bipedalism evolved as a result of wading in water to keep the head above the surface. Turn-Over Pulse Hypothesis: Attributes bipedalism to environmental changes that forced early hominins to adapt to open grasslands.
